name: Scar massage

card.summary: Manual rubbing or pressure on a healed scar to soften it; widely recommended in clinics, with only weak evidence of benefit.
card.note: Reviews describe inconsistent methods and low-quality studies.

quick.overview:
Scar massage means applying repeated manual pressure or movement to a scar, often after wound closure, with the aim of softening it, flattening it and relieving tightness or itch. Surgeons, burn units and physical therapists commonly recommend it.
Reviews of the literature generally find the evidence thin. Wikipedia cites a 2012 review reporting weak evidence of benefit, mainly for surgical incision scars, and a 2022 scoping review of 25 studies that reported favourable outcomes but inconsistent methods.
quick.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms include mechanically remodelling collagen, and other effects on scar tissue; the mechanism and supporting evidence are unclear.
quick.risks: Massage is generally regarded as low risk, but reviews note that regimens vary greatly in timing, duration and technique, which limits conclusions. Open or healing wounds are typically handled under clinical guidance.

lead: Scar massage is the manual application of pressure, stretching or circular movement to a scar, usually after the wound has closed, with the aim of making it softer, flatter, more flexible and less noticeable, and of easing tightness and itch [1][2]. People do it at home with their fingers, often with a lotion or oil, and clinicians such as surgeons, burn therapists and hand therapists teach it as part of aftercare [3][6].

For appearance, the stated goal is a scar that blends better with the surrounding skin: lower profile, less rigid, and less visible on the face or body. Proponents describe massage as a low-cost step that can be combined with silicone sheets or gels and other scar-care measures [1][4].

Published reviews describe a body of mostly small studies with varied protocols. A 2012 review found that 27 of 30 surgical scars treated with massage showed improved appearance, a 2022 scoping review of 25 studies reported favourable outcomes in all of them, and a 2023 meta-analysis pooled seven burn-scar studies; reviewers also note inconsistent methods and outcome measures [2][5][6].

paras: Scar massage covers a range of techniques, from circular rubbing with the fingertips to deeper stretching or manipulation of the tissue, sometimes with a lotion or oil to reduce friction. A review of regimens found they differed in time to onset, scar location, duration and technique [2]. Studied protocols ranged from about 10 minutes twice daily to 30 minutes twice weekly, with onset from soon after suture removal to more than two years after injury, and duration from a single treatment to six months [2].

Massage is often combined with other scar-management measures such as silicone products and pressure garments, which complicates assessment of its separate effect [1]. In rehabilitation, related manual techniques are also used for scar-related tightness after breast surgery, such as axillary web syndrome [7][8].

sections.h: Appearance goals and who uses it
paras: The appearance goals people describe are a flatter scar, a softer scar that moves with the skin, and less redness, itch and tightness. Because scars lack sweat glands and hair follicles and have more aligned collagen than normal skin [9], they often differ visibly from surrounding skin; massage is offered as one way to improve texture and pliability, particularly on visible sites such as the face, neck, hands and chest.

Users include people recovering from surgery, burns, injuries and acne. Burn units, surgeons and hand therapists teach it, and burn-focused reviews note that massage is used in burn units worldwide for functional and cosmetic outcomes [3]. Breast-surgery rehabilitation also uses related manual techniques for tightness [7][8].

Wikipedia describes scar formation as a sequence in which a clot is replaced by a temporary matrix, fibroblasts then produce collagen that cross-links into dense, inelastic tissue, and myofibroblasts drive wound contraction and usually disappear within about 30 days, although they persist in keloids [9]. A wound is not counted as a scar until it has fully healed, which can take months or, in severe cases, years; very small wounds under about 2 mm often heal without scarring and rapid healing within about two weeks also tends to limit it [9].

Mechanical tension is named as a leading cause of hypertrophic scars, which tend to form after injuries that reach deep into the dermis, such as burns, piercings and cuts [11]. Hypertrophic scars can keep rising for up to six months and usually fade over one to two years [11]. This timeline is the backdrop for massage protocols, which are usually described as aimed at the early, still-remodelling scar.

sections.h: Scar types and the aim of massage
paras: Wikipedia describes a scar as fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin after injury, with collagen fibres that are more aligned and cross-linked than in uninjured skin, and notes that scars lack sweat glands and hair follicles [9]. Common types include hypertrophic scars (raised, red or dark, within the wound boundary), keloids (growing beyond the original wound), atrophic scars (sunken, often after acne) and stretch marks [9]. Hypertrophic scars usually appear within 4 to 8 weeks of wound closure [9].

Massage is mostly studied on surgical incision scars and hypertrophic burn scars; the 2016 evidence review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery considers hypertrophic scars, keloids and stretch marks and discusses massage under hypertrophic scars [1].

Keloids are a more severe form that grows beyond the original wound; they are benign but can itch or hurt, and Wikipedia reports they occur in 15 to 20 per cent of people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latin American ancestry, with about a third of people with keloids having an affected first-degree relative [10]. Surgical excision alone is reported to have a recurrence rate of 70 to 100 per cent, which is why clinicians combine surgery with pressure therapy, radiation or laser [10]. Wikipedia's keloid article does not mention massage as a treatment [10], and pressure therapy is described there as promising after excision of ear keloids [10].

Wikipedia's hypertrophic scar article states that pressure or massage is recommended for early scars during roughly the first one and a half to three months, with silicone gel sheeting, corticosteroid injection, laser, cryosurgery and revision among the other options [11]. Atrophic, sunken scars, often from acne, and stretch marks are other categories people ask about; Wikipedia's stretch-mark article describes no clearly useful treatments and reports no evidence that creams or oils prevent them in pregnancy [12][9].

Proposed mechanisms include mechanical effects on collagen alignment and tissue mobility and, in burn research, mechanotransduction and neurogenic inflammation, concepts highlighted in a recent review of conservative burn-scar treatments [5]. Reviews describe the mechanism and how best to deliver massage as not settled [3][6].

The 2012 Dermatologic Surgery review examined ten publications covering 144 patients who received massage. Overall 65 patients (45.7%) showed clinical improvement on measures such as the Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale, Vancouver Scar Scale, range of motion, itch, pain or mood, and 27 of 30 surgical scars (90%) had improved appearance or scale scores [2]. The authors described the evidence as limited [2].

A 2016 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery rated the strength of evidence for each scar intervention. For preventing hypertrophic scars, silicone, tension reduction and wound-edge eversion were rated high efficacy while scar massage was rated low; for treating existing hypertrophic scars, massage was grouped with silicone, lasers, corticosteroids and others as high efficacy [1].

A 2018 systematic review in Burns noted that massage is used in burn units worldwide to improve functional and cosmetic outcomes, while evidence for it was previously unknown [3]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Clinical Nursing pooled seven studies with 420 burn patients, with sessions lasting 5 to 30 minutes, and described earlier evidence on burn-scar improvement as inconsistent [4]. A 2022 scoping review of 25 studies on post-surgical scars (1,515 participants) reported favourable outcomes in all studies but found 45 different outcome measures, non-standardised assessment, protocols from one session to three daily for six months, and confounding by other rehabilitation in 13 studies [6].

Scar massage is usually one element of a package. Wikipedia lists silicone gel sheeting among the commonly used measures, noting a Cochrane review that found weak, low-quality evidence for preventing scars, and describes pressure dressings as widely used for burn and hypertrophic scars despite limited formal evidence [9]. Stress shielding, meaning reducing mechanical tension across a new wound, is a prevention concept that research links with smaller scars [9].

Clinic-based options include long-term corticosteroid injection for keloids and hypertrophic scars, nonablative lasers for raised scars, ablative lasers and subcision for atrophic and acne scars, chemical peels, fillers, microneedling, low-dose radiotherapy for severe cases and camouflage makeup [9]. Wikipedia also reports that vitamin E and onion extract products showed no benefit in studies, and that a 2021 mouse study found the drug verteporfin enabled scar-free healing by blocking mechanical-stress signalling [9].

Massage is generally described in the reviewed literature as low risk and is used routinely in clinics; the reviews focus on effectiveness rather than harms [2][6]. Timing relative to wound healing varies between protocols, from just after suture removal to long after [2].

Guidance in the clinical literature generally places massage after the wound has closed, and protocols differ on exact timing [2]. Raised scars that keep growing, painful scars and scars after burns are managed by clinicians, and keloid-prone people are advised in sources such as Wikipedia to avoid unnecessary skin trauma [10]. Related manual therapy for conditions such as axillary web syndrome after breast surgery is studied within supervised physiotherapy [7][8].

The main human evidence consists of the following. A 2012 literature review of ten publications and 144 patients [2]. A 2018 systematic review of massage for hypertrophic burn scars [3]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies with 420 burn patients [4]. A 2022 scoping review of 25 studies and 1,515 participants with surgical scars [6]. A 2025 review of conservative burn-scar management that examines evidence for and against common modalities [5]. Related rehabilitation research includes a systematic review of physiotherapy for axillary web syndrome after breast cancer, which concluded that exercise and stretching were most effective and that manual therapy and scar massage might help but with weaker support [7], and a 2025 randomised trial of 46 women using stretching combined with manual therapy and scar massage for that condition [8]. Reviewers repeatedly call for standardised protocols and higher-quality trials.

Scar massage is discussed in appearance and skin-care communities as an inexpensive, at-home step for surgical, acne or injury scars, usually next to silicone products, sun protection and, for deeper scars, procedures such as lasers and microneedling [9]. It sits in the same conversation as acne-scar treatments, where users weigh at-home care against clinic-based resurfacing. No published trial has tested massage for acne scars specifically; the studies are in surgical and burn scars [3][4][6].

lore.intro: Scar massage is recommended in clinic aftercare and home-care advice for surgical, burn and injury scars, and the claims below reflect what is commonly said about it [3][9].

claims.claim: Massage makes scars softer, flatter and less visible
claims.believers: Therapists and patients describe softer, more flexible scars after regular massage, and burn units use it widely for functional and cosmetic goals [3].
claims.experts: A 2012 review found improvement in 27 of 30 surgical scars and a 2022 scoping review reported favourable outcomes in all 25 studies, while both note inconsistent methods and limited evidence [2][6].

claims.believers: Some guidance includes massage in early scar-care routines alongside silicone [11].
claims.experts: A 2016 review rated silicone, tension reduction and wound-edge eversion as high efficacy for prevention and scar massage as low [1].

claims.believers: Burn therapists teach massage for hypertrophic burn scars [3].
claims.experts: A 2018 systematic review noted evidence had been unknown, and a 2023 meta-analysis pooled seven studies of 420 burn patients and called earlier evidence inconsistent [3][4].

claims.believers: Some people try rubbing keloids as part of at-home care.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's keloid article lists pressure therapy, silicone, steroid injection, cryotherapy, radiation and laser as options and does not list massage; excision alone recurs in 70 to 100 per cent of cases [10].

claims.claim: Massage fades acne or atrophic scars
claims.believers: Home-care advice sometimes extends massage to sunken acne scars.
claims.experts: Atrophic scars reflect loss of underlying tissue and Wikipedia lists lasers, subcision, fillers and microneedling for them; studies of massage are in surgical and burn scars [9][6].

claims.claim: Creams and oils prevent stretch marks and scars
claims.believers: Oils and creams are often used with massage, usually to reduce friction.
claims.experts: A systematic review summarised on Wikipedia found no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks in pregnancy, and vitamin E and onion extract showed no benefit for scars [12][9].

angle.text: Scar massage is a hands-on routine people use during scar healing to try to soften and flatten a scar. It targets the scar's texture and flexibility rather than skin colour, and is often used alongside silicone products.
